interview_metadata.name: Kweku Cooper
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised right here around Blountstown, Calhoun County, Florida. My people are African-American Southern folks, church on Sunday, fish fries, helping cousins move, that kind of close-knit life. We did not have a lot extra, but we had structure. My daddy worked with timber and maintenance jobs, and my mama worked in food service and later at a school cafeteria. I finished high school here. I was decent in math and liked things where there was a right answer, but I was not much for sitting in classrooms longer than I had to. I started working different retail and stock jobs after school, and over time I got steady at a regional department store. I have been there about ten years now, mostly sales floor, inventory, returns, cash register, merchandising, and keeping an eye out for theft or fake returns. I never married and do not have children. I have dated, but I am particular about my space and routine. Outside work, I fish the Apalachicola River, restore old wood furniture in my garage, read biographies and historical fiction, play online chess, and sometimes help one student at a time at the community center. I am 40 now, and the big thing in my mind is moving from being the dependable floor guy to being a supervisor, maybe one day managing more than one store or opening a small convenience store of my own.

follow_ups.question: When you think about childhood in Calhoun County, what memories come back first?
follow_ups.response: Hot afternoons, dirt roads, church dinners, my uncles talking under a shade tree, and learning early that if something broke you tried to fix it before buying another one.

follow_ups.question: Who helped shape your work ethic the most?
follow_ups.response: My parents. My daddy was quiet but exact about tools and doing work right, and my mama believed you showed up clean, on time, and respectful no matter what was going on at home.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after high school. I had people telling me I should try community college, and I had other people saying get a job, bring money in, and do not take on debt. I did try to look into classes, but I was already working part time and helping around home. Retail felt practical because I could earn right away. At first I thought it was temporary, but I found out I was good with customers, numbers, and spotting when inventory did not add up. The choice made me steady, but it also put a ceiling over me because a high school diploma only carries you so far. Now I am looking back at that same crossroads from the other side, thinking I need business and inventory courses if I want management.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone push you strongly toward college?
follow_ups.response: One teacher did. She said I had the patience for business classes, but nobody in my house really knew how to walk me through financial aid or paperwork.

follow_ups.question: Do you regret choosing work first?
follow_ups.response: Not exactly. I regret not adding training sooner, but I do not regret learning how stores actually run.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was partly a choice and partly life pulling me. I chose steady work, but I also felt like the road toward college was foggy and the road toward a paycheck was right in front of me.

follow_ups.question: What made the paycheck feel so important then?
follow_ups.response: Gas, food, helping at home, and just wanting to feel grown instead of asking people for money.

follow_ups.question: Would you make the same choice now?
follow_ups.response: I would still work, but I would take one class at a time from the beginning.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. If someone had sat me down with a clear plan for community college, grants, and part-time work, I might have done it. In a small town you hear advice, but not always step-by-step guidance.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Paperwork help and somebody checking in after the first month, not just saying, 'You should go.'

follow_ups.question: Do you try to give that kind of help now?
follow_ups.response: A little. When I tutor, I try to make the next step plain.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner right now, and I do not have children. My immediate family still matters a lot. My mother lives nearby, and I check on her a couple times a week, usually by phone and then in person on Sunday or Monday. My father passed a few years back, and I still think about him when I am working on furniture because he taught me how to respect wood and tools. I have an older sister in Marianna with two kids. We are not in each other's business every day, but if something happens, we show up. I have a few cousins around Calhoun and Jackson County. Family gatherings usually center on church events, cookouts, or somebody needing help with a repair. I keep some distance because I like quiet, but I am not cut off.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do when you visit your mother?
follow_ups.response: I bring groceries if she needs them, check small things around the house, sit a while, and listen to what is going on with church folks.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your sister and her kids?
follow_ups.response: Maybe twice a month, more around birthdays or school events. I am the uncle who brings practical gifts.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a younger brother who lives closer to Tallahassee. We get along, but we are different. He is more social and spontaneous than me.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk with him?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every week or two, usually text unless something serious is going on.

follow_ups.question: What do you two connect over?
follow_ups.response: Sports mostly, especially the Jaguars, and family news.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small circle. There is Marcus, who I fish with sometimes, though a lot of times I go alone. There are a couple coworkers I trust, especially Denise at customer service because she knows returns better than anybody. I also know men through the Riverbend Anglers Club and a community softball group. I am friendly with people, but I do not need a crowd. If I am spending time with somebody, it is usually fishing, talking sports, helping move furniture, or meeting for breakfast before work.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a closest friend?
follow_ups.response: Marcus is probably closest. We can sit on the riverbank for an hour without forcing conversation.

follow_ups.question: Are you dating anyone?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now. I have dated, but I am not actively looking every week.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Blountstown, in a modest rental house on a quiet street. It is the kind of place where people notice whose truck is in the driveway. You have woods, churches, small businesses, and the river not too far off. There are not many fancy restaurants or big-city things, but I like that I can get to work, the grocery store, my mother's place, and fishing spots without fighting traffic. Some houses are kept up better than others. Money is tight for a lot of people around here, and you can see it in old roofs, patched cars, and people doing side work.

follow_ups.question: Who do you know on your street?
follow_ups.response: I know my next-door neighbor Mr. Lanier and a woman across the street named Miss Carla. We wave, talk weather, and keep an eye out.

follow_ups.question: What places do you go most near home?
follow_ups.response: Work, church with my mother some Sundays, the grocery store, the river landing, and the hardware store.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I lock my doors and do not leave tools out, but I am not scared walking to my truck at night.

follow_ups.question: What makes you cautious?
follow_ups.response: Petty theft mostly. Tools, gas cans, packages, things like that can disappear.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for each other?
follow_ups.response: Yes, quietly. People notice strange cars and will call or text.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is familiarity, low pace, family nearby, and access to the river. The downside is limited opportunity, lower wages, and having to drive if you need specialized health care or more choices.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: Family, cost, and the land. I know how to live here.

follow_ups.question: What would make you leave?
follow_ups.response: A serious management job or opening my own store somewhere nearby, not too far.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live by myself. It is a two-bedroom rental, though the second room is more storage and books than bedroom. My garage is where I keep furniture projects, clamps, sandpaper, and old chairs I swear I am going to finish. I like living alone because after working retail all day, I need quiet. Nobody is staying with me right now.

follow_ups.question: Do family members ever stay overnight?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. A nephew might crash if there is a family thing, but not regular.

follow_ups.question: How do you use your space day to day?
follow_ups.response: Kitchen, bedroom, living room for reading and chess, and garage for furniture work.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me, permanently.

follow_ups.question: Anyone expected to move in soon?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Would you want a roommate?
follow_ups.response: Not unless money forced it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Nobody stays here regularly.

follow_ups.question: Any visiting relatives?
follow_ups.response: Only occasional overnight family, maybe once or twice a year.

follow_ups.question: Any regular guests?
follow_ups.response: No, mostly short visits.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: No one away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No college student or worker away?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week depends on the store schedule. If I open, I am up around 5:45, coffee, quick breakfast, and at work before 7:30. If I close, I start later and get home around 9:30 or 10. On weekdays I usually cook simple food, check on my mother by phone, play chess online, or sand furniture for an hour. Saturday might be work, fishing, or errands depending on the schedule. Sunday morning I may go to church with my mother, then cook a bigger meal or watch baseball or football depending on the season.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to sleep?
follow_ups.response: Around 11 on normal nights, later after a closing shift.

follow_ups.question: What is your most settled routine?
follow_ups.response: Coffee in the morning, checking my bank app, and keeping a written list of bills and errands.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a retail sales associate at a regional department store. I handle customers, stocking, price checks, returns, register backup, merchandising, inventory counts, and sometimes loss prevention type situations when something seems off. My schedule changes, but I usually work five days a week, about 38 to 40 hours. Shifts can be 7:30 to 4, 10 to 6, or 1 to close. Holidays and back-to-school season are busier, and that is when I watch sales numbers closely because I want management to see I can hit targets.

follow_ups.question: Which department do you work most?
follow_ups.response: Mostly home goods and seasonal, with some time in apparel when they need coverage.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job are you best at?
follow_ups.response: Finding inventory problems and matching customers with something that actually fits their need.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep my own house, cook most of my meals, and help my mother with errands. Twice a month or so I tutor at the community center, usually one student in math or reading. I also keep up with my truck because I cannot afford surprise repairs. On payday I sit down with bills, savings, and grocery plans before I spend on anything extra.

follow_ups.question: What do you cook most often?
follow_ups.response: Catfish, rice, greens, shrimp and grits if I find shrimp at a decent price, and baked pork shoulder when family is coming.

follow_ups.question: How often do you tutor?
follow_ups.response: Usually every other Wednesday evening, depending on my work schedule.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Recently I have been trying to act more like the supervisor I want to become. I started writing down stock issues and sales numbers instead of just fixing things quietly. I also signed up for information about a short online business management course, though I have not started yet. At home I have cut back on late-night scrolling and chess because I was staying up too late after closing shifts.

follow_ups.question: What pushed that change?
follow_ups.response: A younger coworker got promoted elsewhere, and it made me realize time keeps moving whether I prepare or not.

follow_ups.question: Has it helped?
follow_ups.response: Some. My manager has noticed my notes, and I feel less like I am just drifting.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have that routine myself. I do hear about school schedules through my sister's kids and the tutoring program, but I am not the one getting children up or handling after-school activities.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with your niece or nephew's routines?
follow_ups.response: Only occasionally, like picking one up if my sister is stuck.

follow_ups.question: Do kids play a regular role in your life?
follow_ups.response: Mostly as an uncle and occasional tutor, not daily.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My own experiences have mostly been traffic stops and seeing deputies around town. I have been pulled over for a taillight and for speeding a little, and I kept my hands visible and answered straight. Being a Black man in a small Southern town, you learn to stay calm even when you feel irritated. At work we sometimes call law enforcement for theft or disorderly customers, and I try to be factual, not dramatic.

follow_ups.question: Have you felt treated fairly in those stops?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes fair, sometimes like I had to prove I was harmless first.

follow_ups.question: Has work changed how you see policing?
follow_ups.response: It made me see they deal with real problems, but also that attitude and discretion matter a lot.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: After a storm, deputies helped direct traffic near downed trees, and that was useful. Another time a cousin got stopped and searched, and the explanation sounded thin to me.

follow_ups.question: Did your cousin face charges?
follow_ups.response: No, nothing came of it, which is part of why it bothered us.

follow_ups.question: Do people in your family talk about these things?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but usually at home, not loudly in public.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have had distant relatives with arrests, mostly drug or probation trouble, but not my immediate household.

follow_ups.question: Did those arrests affect your family?
follow_ups.response: They affected gatherings and money sometimes, but not my day-to-day household.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about younger relatives?
follow_ups.response: I do. I tell them one bad decision can follow you for years.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and most midterms, but I have missed local elections when work got in the way or I did not know enough about the candidates. I am trying to do better with local races because those decisions hit roads, schools, policing, and taxes. I do not put campaign signs in my yard, but I do pay attention.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide who to vote for?
follow_ups.response: I look at jobs, health care, schools, fairness, and whether the person sounds practical or just loud.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early or on Election Day?
follow_ups.response: Usually early if my schedule is unpredictable.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself moderate, leaning Democratic. I care about working people, fair wages, health care access, and not treating poor towns like we do not matter. On race and policing, I think there are real problems that people want to brush aside. At the same time, I am practical and skeptical of big promises from either party. I believe in personal responsibility because I was raised that way, but I also know a person can work hard and still get boxed in by low wages, bad schools, medical bills, or who they know. I do not like politics as entertainment. I want roads fixed, stores open, hospitals reachable, and kids having a better shot.

follow_ups.question: What issues feel most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Wages, health care, rural investment, and fair treatment by police and employers.

follow_ups.question: Do your coworkers share your views?
follow_ups.response: Some do, some do not. I usually keep politics light at work unless I know the person can talk respectfully.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten more focused on local government and less impressed by national arguing. During the last few years, I saw how supply chains, health rules, wages, and housing all hit regular people fast. I also started thinking more about small businesses because I may want one. So I still lean Democratic, but I listen for who understands small-town economics, not just party labels.

follow_ups.question: Has owning a store changed your thinking?
follow_ups.response: It has made me think about taxes, insurance, theft, wages, and how hard it is to run lean.

follow_ups.question: Any issue you changed your mind on?
follow_ups.response: I used to ignore county meetings. Now I think those matter more than I gave them credit for.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat to a lot. It did not teach me racism existed; I already knew that from family stories and my own life. What it did was make more people talk openly about things Black folks have talked about privately for years. I agreed with the concern about accountability, but I did not join every slogan or argument online. I wanted the focus to stay on fair treatment and real policy.

follow_ups.question: Did it change conversations in your family?
follow_ups.response: Yes. My mother talked about older times, and younger relatives talked about phone videos and fear during traffic stops.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect how you act around police?
follow_ups.response: I was already careful. It just made me more aware of how many people had similar stories.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the main issue is accountability and equal value. If a police officer does wrong, the badge should not erase consequences. I also think communities need safety, so the answer cannot be pretending crime does not hurt people. In my mind, you can want fair policing and still want quick help when somebody is breaking into cars. Those two things should not be enemies.

follow_ups.question: What reforms make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Body cameras used consistently, better training, real review boards, and getting rid of officers with repeated complaints.

follow_ups.question: What worries you about the debate?
follow_ups.response: People turn it into teams and stop listening to the actual problem.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is still tied into money, schools, housing, health, and who gets believed. Around here, people may not always say ugly things out loud, but old patterns are still there. I also think Black families have a lot of resilience and culture that does not get talked about enough unless something bad happens. I try not to live angry, but I do not pretend everything is equal.

follow_ups.question: Where do you see those patterns locally?
follow_ups.response: Who owns land, who gets hired into better jobs, which neighborhoods get attention, and how some people are watched in stores.

follow_ups.question: What gives you hope?
follow_ups.response: Younger people mix more easily, and some are more willing to call unfairness what it is.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I talked with family and a few trusted friends. I did not join protests. I mostly kept my thoughts off social media because arguments there go sideways fast.

follow_ups.question: Why not protest?
follow_ups.response: Partly work, partly personality. I am not a crowd person.

follow_ups.question: Do you speak up at work?
follow_ups.response: Only if somebody says something clearly wrong. Then I keep it plain.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My mother is more prayerful and cautious. She says we have seen hard times before and have to keep dignity. My sister is more direct, especially because she has kids and worries about them driving one day. My brother posts more online than I do. Friends are mixed: some are fired up, some are tired, and some just want life to be less tense.

follow_ups.question: Do these differences cause conflict?
follow_ups.response: Not much. We may disagree on tone, but we agree fairness matters.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk to most about it?
follow_ups.response: My sister and Marcus.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is decent. I am not a gym person, but I stay active at work, lifting boxes, walking the floor, and fishing on weekends. I could lose some weight and eat less fried food. My blood pressure has been borderline at times, so I try to watch salt when I am paying attention. No major disability or serious diagnosis that keeps me from working.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: I have a clinic I use, but I am not as regular as I should be.

follow_ups.question: What exercise do you actually enjoy?
follow_ups.response: Fishing, walking by the river, and occasional pickup softball.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when I cook at home and keep a routine. It is hard when I close late, get hungry, and grab something salty or fried. Blountstown is not full of health options, and healthier groceries cost more. Work keeps me moving, but it also wears out my feet and back.

follow_ups.question: What healthy meal do you make?
follow_ups.response: Pan-seared catfish with lemon butter, dill, rice, and greens, not too heavy.

follow_ups.question: What is your weak spot?
follow_ups.response: Gas station snacks after late shifts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge. I had a spell of lower back pain after moving patio furniture displays at work, and it took a couple weeks of heat pads and being careful. I also had a clinic visit where they told me to watch my blood pressure. That got my attention, but I have not been put on daily medicine. Mostly it is normal wear and tear.

follow_ups.question: Did the back pain make you miss work?
follow_ups.response: I missed one day and then worked lighter tasks for a short while.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed anything for blood pressure?
follow_ups.response: Less sausage, less canned food, and I try to drink more water.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working long term. Back pain slowed me down, and tired feet are real, but I can still do my job.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about future health limiting work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, retail is hard on the body, which is another reason I want management.

follow_ups.question: Any accommodations at work?
follow_ups.response: No formal ones.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, mainly my mother. She has diabetes and blood pressure issues, and I help her keep track of appointments and groceries. My sister does more of the hands-on scheduling, but I help with rides or picking up medicine when I can. My father's health before he passed also taught me that men can ignore symptoms too long.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help your mother medically?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month directly, plus phone reminders.

follow_ups.question: Does it affect your work schedule?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I ask for a certain morning off for an appointment.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Health care around here can be a hassle. Basic clinic care is available, but specialists mean driving, waiting, and figuring out cost. I have delayed dental work because it was expensive. I have also waited out minor things longer than I should because I did not want a bill. Insurance through work helps some, but copays and deductibles still make you think twice.

follow_ups.question: What care have you put off most?
follow_ups.response: Dental and routine checkups.

follow_ups.question: What helps you get care when needed?
follow_ups.response: Planning appointments around work and using the clinic instead of the emergency room.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing formal like that, but we do use home remedies. My mother believes in ginger tea, honey, lemon, Epsom salt soaks, and certain foods when you feel run down. I will use heat, stretching, and old-fashioned common sense before going to the doctor for every ache. But if something is serious, I believe in medical care.

follow_ups.question: Any remedy you personally use?
follow_ups.response: Epsom salt for sore feet and ginger tea when my stomach is off.

follow_ups.question: Do you distrust doctors?
follow_ups.response: No. I just watch costs and do not run in for every little thing.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink occasionally, maybe a beer while watching a game or at a cookout. When I am stressed, I am more likely to go fishing, work in the garage, or play chess too late. I have seen alcohol cause problems in families, so I keep a line around it.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: A couple beers a month, sometimes none.

follow_ups.question: What is your main stress outlet?
follow_ups.response: Fishing alone early in the morning.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other drugs. For pain I might take ibuprofen or acetaminophen like the bottle says. When my back hurt, I used over-the-counter medicine, heat patches, and rest. I am cautious with pills because I have seen people get too comfortable taking things they do not need.

follow_ups.question: Any prescribed medications?
follow_ups.response: No daily prescriptions for me right now.

follow_ups.question: When was the last pain medicine use?
follow_ups.response: Probably ibuprofen after a long shift lifting seasonal stock.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I use my job insurance when I need to, and I budget for copays the same way I budget for truck maintenance. My mother has Medicare, and my sister helps her understand bills. We compare pharmacy prices when we can. Nobody is living easy with health costs, but we manage by planning and delaying what does not feel urgent.

follow_ups.question: Do medical costs worry you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially if something major happened.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep emergency savings for health?
follow_ups.response: Some of my rainy-day fund is for that.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally in favor of vaccines, but I like to read reliable information first. I got the COVID vaccine because I work with the public and did not want to put my mother at risk.

follow_ups.question: Did you have concerns?
follow_ups.response: I had normal questions about side effects, but not enough to avoid it.

follow_ups.question: Do you get flu shots?
follow_ups.response: Some years, especially if work is pushing them and it is convenient.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my clinic, pharmacists, and information from public health sources more than social media. I will listen to family concerns, but I verify. I am skeptical by nature, so if somebody sends me a dramatic post, I look for where it came from. My mother's doctor also matters because her health risk is different from mine.

follow_ups.question: Do you use Facebook for health info?

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for local operations connected to timber and general maintenance. Some places processed or moved wood products, and some were businesses that needed repairs and upkeep. It was the kind of work common in rural North Florida.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape your interest in timber craftsmanship?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made me respect wood and the people who know how to work it.

follow_ups.question: Did he like the work?

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am in a supervisor role or assistant manager position, with a steadier schedule and better pay. I want to take business management and inventory analytics courses so I am not just relying on experience. I would like to own a small house with a garage big enough for furniture work. I still want to fish the river and stay close enough to help my mother. Longer term, I keep thinking about a modest neighborhood convenience store that is clean, well-stocked, and run with common sense. I also want to take a real road trip to the Florida Keys for fishing, visit Savannah for history, and someday see the Scottish Highlands for the woodworking and landscape.

follow_ups.question: What is the first concrete step?
follow_ups.response: Enroll in a short business course and talk to my manager about a supervisor track.

follow_ups.question: What do you want to keep the same?
follow_ups.response: My independence, family ties, fishing, and quiet time.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value steadiness, family, self-respect, and doing work right. I value being able to stand on my own without forgetting who helped raise me. I also value quiet because it lets me think. Whether it is a store shelf, a chess move, a piece of furniture, or a fishing line, I like patience and precision. I want my life to show that a person can be modest and still be serious about excellence.

follow_ups.question: What does self-respect mean to you?
follow_ups.response: Keeping your word, paying what you owe, and not acting smaller than you are.

follow_ups.question: What do you want people to know about you?
follow_ups.response: That I may be quiet, but I notice details and I show up.
